pairs.A: DROID addresses the challenge of collecting manipulation demonstrations across varied scenes while retaining a reproducible robot control setup. We present a distributed manipulation dataset and portable collection platform shared by 13 institutions. Common Franka Panda hardware supports reproducible collection across sites, while camera calibration, scene-specific task sampling and periodic environment changes are used to broaden coverage. The dataset contains 76,000 successful episodes; the collection spans 564 scenes and 350 hours. Hardware and software instructions, visualization tools and policy-training resources accompany the release. We evaluate the data using existing language-conditioned diffusion policies on six tasks in four locations, all with DROID hardware. We compare in-domain-only training against equal mixtures of in-domain demonstrations with either successful DROID trajectories or a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture, holding the policy backbone fixed. With ten rollouts per method and task setting, DROID co-training exceeds the next-best method in across-task mean success rate by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. These results support supplementary training with DROID for the evaluated tasks and scene changes.
pairs.B: DROID addresses the joint demands of scene-diverse manipulation data and reproducible collection through a distributed dataset and a shared, portable robot platform. Across 13 institutions, collectors use VR teleoperation, calibrate cameras for each scene, and receive tasks randomly sampled from a feasible task list; periodic prompts vary viewpoints and scene conditions to broaden coverage. The release contains 76,000 successful episodes from 564 scenes in 52 buildings, together with collection and policy-training resources. Evaluation uses existing language-conditioned diffusion policies for six tasks at four locations on the shared hardware, holding the backbone fixed across training conditions. Co-training mixes successful DROID trajectories and in-domain demonstrations 50/50, with alternatives using in-domain data alone or an equal mixture with curated Open X-Embodiment data. DROID co-training yields mean success 22 percentage points above the next-best alternative in-distribution and 17 points above it on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. A size-matched subset comparison further supports a role for scene diversity on the challenging shifted tasks studied.

pairs.A: DROID uses a portable Franka Panda setup with external and wrist stereo cameras and VR teleoperation to keep collection reproducible across institutions while allowing scenes to change. Collectors calibrate cameras and list feasible tasks for each scene, then receive a randomly sampled task for each episode. Periodic prompts vary camera placement, lighting, clutter, or base position to broaden coverage rather than favor easy tasks. Evaluation trains separate language-conditioned diffusion policies for six tasks on the shared hardware, holding the backbone fixed across training conditions. DROID co-training mixes successful dataset trajectories with in-domain demonstrations 50/50; alternatives use in-domain data alone or a 50/50 mixture with curated Open X-Embodiment data. Ten rollouts per method and task setting compare success with perturbed initial robot and object positions and under task-specific shifts involving distractors, new manipulated objects, or camera placement.
pairs.B: DROID uses shared Franka Panda hardware to keep robot control reproducible across collection sites while a portable platform enables scene changes. Collectors operate through VR teleoperation with two adjustable external stereo cameras and a wrist stereo camera. For each scene, they position and calibrate cameras and enter feasible tasks. Random assignment selects the task for each episode, while periodic prompts encourage changes in camera placement, lighting, clutter or base position. To evaluate successful DROID trajectories as supplementary training data, we train separate language-conditioned diffusion policies for six tasks across four locations on DROID hardware. With the same backbone, we compare in-domain-only training with equal mixtures of in-domain demonstrations and either DROID trajectories or curated Open X-Embodiment data. Ten rollouts per method and task setting cover perturbed robot and object positions in-distribution and task-specific out-of-distribution variants.

pairs.A: Across the six evaluated tasks, DROID co-training achieves a higher mean success rate than in-domain-only training or co-training with curated Open X-Embodiment data. All methods use the same diffusion-policy backbone, and both co-training regimes mix supplementary trajectories equally with in-domain demonstrations. With ten rollouts per method and task setting on DROID hardware, DROID co-training exceeds the next-best method by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. Error bars report standard errors around the across-task mean success rates. A size-matched comparison examines scene coverage: with 7,362 successful demonstrations per subset and 50/50 in-domain co-training, the uniformly sampled, more scene-diverse subset outperforms the subset from the 20 most represented scenes on the challenging out-of-distribution tasks studied. This comparison supports a role for scene diversity beyond subset size, without isolating it from all other differences.
pairs.B: Across six tasks at four locations on DROID hardware, 50/50 co-training with successful DROID trajectories and in-domain demonstrations yields mean success 22 percentage points above the next-best alternative in-distribution and 17 points above it on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. Comparators use the same policy backbone with in-domain data alone or a 50/50 mixture of in-domain and curated Open X-Embodiment data. Each method and task setting is evaluated with ten rollouts. To examine scene coverage separately from subset size, a further comparison uses 7,362 successful demonstrations in each subset and equal mixing with in-domain data. A uniformly sampled, more scene-diverse subset performs better on the challenging shifted tasks studied than one drawn from the 20 most represented scenes. This comparison supports a role for scene diversity beyond demonstration count, although it does not isolate every other difference between the subsets.

pairs.A: Collecting manipulation data across diverse scenes requires consistent robot control across collection sites. We present DROID, a distributed manipulation dataset and reproducible collection platform used at 13 institutions. A shared portable Franka Panda system enables collectors to change scenes while retaining common hardware. Within each scene, collectors calibrate cameras and teleoperate randomly sampled feasible tasks; periodic prompts vary camera placement, lighting, clutter, or robot base position. The dataset contains 76,000 successful episodes spanning 564 scenes, accompanied by crowdsourced language instructions. We release collection instructions and policy-training resources alongside the data. Evaluation uses existing language-conditioned diffusion policies trained separately for six tasks in four locations on DROID hardware. Mixing in-domain demonstrations and successful DROID trajectories equally yields higher mean success than in-domain-only training or equal-share co-training with a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture. All three conditions use the same policy backbone. Across the six tasks, the gains over the next-best method are 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 under task-specific out-of-distribution changes. A fixed-size subset comparison further supports scene diversity on the challenging shifted tasks studied.
pairs.B: DROID combines a distributed manipulation dataset with a portable collection platform to gather demonstrations across varied scenes. The shared Franka Panda setup supports reproducible control across 13 institutions; portability, randomized task assignment, and prompts to vary scene conditions broaden collection coverage. The dataset contains 76,000 successful episodes with language annotations; unsuccessful trajectories are also released but excluded from co-training. Utility is evaluated with separate diffusion policies for six tasks in four locations on DROID hardware. With a common policy backbone, in-domain-only training is compared against 50/50 co-training using either successful DROID trajectories or a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture. DROID co-training exceeds the next-best method in across-task mean success rate by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 percentage points on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. A count-matched subset comparison also favors broader scene diversity on the challenging shifted tasks studied. These results support the dataset's utility alongside in-domain demonstrations on the evaluated hardware and tasks.

pairs.A: DROID uses a shared, portable Franka Panda platform with external and wrist stereo cameras and VR teleoperation, allowing scene changes on a reproducible robot setup. For each new scene, collectors calibrate cameras and specify feasible tasks, from which the task for each episode is randomly sampled. Periodic prompts ask collectors to vary camera placement, lighting, clutter, or base position to broaden coverage rather than favor easy tasks. Crowdsourced annotators provide up to three independent language instructions per episode. To evaluate the data, separate language-conditioned diffusion policies are trained for six tasks across four locations on DROID hardware. Training uses a common backbone and either in-domain demonstrations alone or 50/50 co-training with successful DROID trajectories or a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture. Tests use ten rollouts per method and task setting, covering perturbed in-distribution starts and task-specific out-of-distribution variants with new objects, distractors, or shifted cameras.
pairs.B: A portable Franka Panda platform with two adjustable external stereo cameras, a wrist stereo camera, and VR teleoperation standardizes DROID collection while allowing scene changes. Collectors position and calibrate cameras in each scene, enter feasible tasks, and receive a randomly sampled task for each episode. Periodic prompts vary camera placement, lighting, clutter, or base position to broaden coverage. To evaluate the data, separate language-conditioned diffusion policies are trained for six tasks in four locations. DROID co-training mixes in-domain demonstrations and successful DROID trajectories equally, excluding unsuccessful trajectories from training. Comparators use the same backbone with either in-domain demonstrations alone or equal-share co-training with a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture. Each method and task setting receives ten rollouts on DROID hardware, testing perturbed initial robot and object positions within the demonstration distribution and task-specific out-of-distribution changes.

pairs.A: With the diffusion-policy backbone unchanged, DROID co-training produced higher across-task mean success than in-domain-only training or co-training with a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture. Both co-training conditions mixed in-domain demonstrations and supplementary trajectories equally; only successful DROID trajectories entered training. Across six tasks in four locations on DROID hardware, DROID exceeded the next-best method by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 under task-specific out-of-distribution shifts. The main comparison used ten rollouts per method and task setting; reported error bars represent standard error around across-task means. The scene-diversity check used two subsets of 7,362 successful demonstrations, each mixed equally with in-domain data. Uniformly sampled trajectories spanning more scenes outperformed trajectories from the 20 most represented scenes on the challenging shifted tasks studied. This secondary comparison supports a role for scene diversity, but does not isolate it from other subset differences.
pairs.B: With the policy backbone held fixed, DROID co-training yields higher across-task mean success rates than in-domain-only training or co-training with a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture. Each co-training mixture contains equal parts in-domain and auxiliary data, with the DROID portion restricted to successful trajectories. Across six tasks in four locations on DROID hardware, its mean success rate exceeds the next-best comparator by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 on task-specific out-of-distribution variants, with ten rollouts per method and task setting. A separate comparison uses 7,362 successful demonstrations per subset in 50/50 in-domain co-training. Policies co-trained with a uniformly sampled, more scene-diverse subset perform better than those using a subset from the 20 most represented scenes on the challenging shifted tasks studied. Fixing the demonstration count supports a role for scene diversity beyond quantity, although other differences between the subsets are not fully isolated.

pairs.A: SIMPLER is a simulated evaluation framework for comparing policies trained on real robot data, emphasizing relative performance and behavioral differences rather than exact physical success rates. To align action effects, it replays actions from existing demonstrations and tunes controller stiffness and damping against end-effector trajectory mismatch. Visual Matching addresses visual mismatch by compositing simulated robots and interactive objects onto an inpainted real-scene background and adjusting their textures. The framework also measures ranking errors using Mean Maximum Rank Violation, which averages each policy's largest misranking margin in real-world success rates. For six checkpoints across three Google Robot task groups, Visual Matching yields average MMRV of 0.056, compared with 0.143 for Variant Aggregation over randomized visual environments and 0.375 for validation action MSE. Simulation also suggests greater arm-texture sensitivity for Octo-Base than RT-1-X, a relative difference supported by new physical arm-wrapping experiments. These comparisons support simulation as a signal for policy ranking and robustness analysis within the evaluated rigid-body setups.
pairs.B: We introduce SIMPLER, a simulated evaluation framework for comparing policies trained on real robot data despite discrepancies in control and appearance. Its target is relative performance, not exact reproduction of real-world success rates. Existing demonstration actions are replayed to tune simulated controllers against real end-effector motion. Visual Matching composites segmented simulated robots and interactive objects onto an inpainted real background and adjusts textures to align their appearance. Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV) averages each policy's largest real-world success-rate margin involved in a simulator misranking; lower values indicate better ranking agreement. Across six policy checkpoints and three Google Robot task groups, Visual Matching yields average MMRV of 0.056, compared with 0.143 for Variant Aggregation, which averages outcomes across randomized visual variants, and 0.375 for rankings based on validation action mean squared error. WidowX comparisons yield task-averaged MMRV of 0.014. These results support relative policy evaluation in the tested, mainly rigid-body setups, while some checkpoints remain sensitive to visual differences. The open-source release provides environments and construction guidance for reuse.

pairs.A: SIMPLER pairs simulated and physical evaluations of policies trained on real data in Google Robot and WidowX setups, mainly for rigid-body tasks. It aligns action effects by replaying actions from existing real demonstrations and tuning controller stiffness and damping through simulated annealing to reduce end-effector translation and rotation mismatch; no new demonstrations are collected for this step. Visual Matching composites segmented simulated robots and interactive objects with an inpainted real-scene background, then adjusts or projects textures to align their appearance. Variant Aggregation instead averages outcomes over randomized visual environments. To assess whether simulated outcomes preserve physical policy ordering, Mean Maximum Rank Violation averages each policy's largest misranking margin in real-world success rates. Pearson correlation provides a complementary measure, since correlation alone can misrepresent nonlinear but order-preserving performance or noisy comparisons within a narrow range.
pairs.B: SIMPLER constructs SAPIEN evaluations for Google Robot and WidowX policies trained on real data, focusing mainly on rigid-body tasks. System identification first replays actions from existing real demonstrations and compares simulated and real end-effector translation and rotation. Simulated annealing adjusts controller stiffness and damping to reduce this mismatch, aligning action effects without training a replacement policy. Visual Matching then composites segmented simulated robots and interactive objects onto an inpainted real background and adjusts or projects textures. Variant Aggregation provides an alternative by averaging evaluation outcomes across randomized visual variants. Paired real and simulated evaluations assess policy-ranking agreement. Mean Maximum Rank Violation averages, across policies, each policy's largest real-world success-rate margin involved in a simulator misranking; lower values indicate better agreement. Pearson correlation separately measures linear association, which need not capture ranking fidelity.

pairs.A: For six policy checkpoints across three Google Robot task groups, Visual Matching provides better agreement with physical policy ordering than Variant Aggregation or validation action MSE. Average Mean Maximum Rank Violation is 0.056, compared with 0.143 and 0.375 for the two alternatives, respectively; mean Pearson correlation is also higher, at 0.924 versus 0.778 and 0.308. The MMRV contrast favors Visual Matching when ranking errors are judged by the physical performance gap between misordered policies. A separate check connects simulated robustness patterns to physical behavior: Octo-Base appears more sensitive to arm texture than RT-1-X in simulation, and new real-world arm-wrapping experiments support that relative sensitivity. Together, these comparisons support simulation as an informative ranking and behavioral evaluation signal for the tested policies and rigid-body setups, rather than exact success-rate reproduction.
pairs.B: Visual Matching tracks real-world policy ordering more closely than Variant Aggregation or rankings based on validation action mean squared error across six policy checkpoints and three Google Robot task groups. Average Mean Maximum Rank Violation, which penalizes reversals by their real-world success-rate margins, is 0.056 for Visual Matching, versus 0.143 and 0.375 for the alternatives, respectively; lower values indicate closer ranking agreement. Mean Pearson correlations are 0.924, 0.778 and 0.308 in the same order. The comparison supports visually matched simulation as a better ranking signal in these task groups than either variant averaging or validation action error. A secondary check tests a behavioral prediction: simulation suggests that Octo-Base is more sensitive to arm texture than RT-1-X, and real-world arm-wrapping experiments support this relative sensitivity. Thus, the agreement extends to a specific visual robustness pattern, not to exact success-rate reproduction for every policy or task.

pairs.A: SIMPLER provides a simulated evaluation framework for robot policies trained on real data, targeting relative performance rather than exact real-world success rates. To reduce control mismatch, it replays actions from existing real demonstrations in simulation and tunes controller parameters against recorded end-effector trajectories. Visual Matching addresses appearance by compositing simulated robots and interactive objects with inpainted real-scene backgrounds and adjusting their textures. These procedures are implemented in SAPIEN task setups for Google Robot and WidowX. Mean Maximum Rank Violation penalizes policy misordering by real-world success-rate margins, complementing Pearson correlation. Across six policy checkpoints and three Google Robot task groups, average rank violation is 0.056 for Visual Matching, 0.143 for Variant Aggregation over randomized visual environments, and 0.375 for validation action mean squared error. Simulation also indicates greater arm-texture sensitivity in Octo-Base than RT-1-X, a relative difference supported by subsequent real robot arm-wrapping experiments. The results support comparative policy evaluation and behavioral diagnosis in the tested, mainly rigid-body settings.
pairs.B: Control and visual discrepancies complicate simulated evaluation of policies trained on real robot data. We present SIMPLER, a framework for comparing relative policy performance and behavior rather than reproducing exact physical success rates. It replays actions from existing real demonstrations and tunes controller stiffness and damping to reduce mismatch between simulated and real end-effector motion. Visual Matching combines simulated robots and interactive objects with an inpainted real-scene background, then adjusts robot and object textures to better match their real counterparts. Mean Maximum Rank Violation measures ranking disagreement through the real-world success-rate margins of misordered policy pairs. Policies are evaluated on Google Robot and WidowX hardware and in corresponding SAPIEN setups, primarily on rigid-body tasks. For six policy checkpoints across three Google Robot task groups, average rank violation is 0.056 with Visual Matching, compared with 0.143 for averaging randomized visual variants and 0.375 for validation action mean squared error. Physical arm-wrapping experiments also support simulation's suggestion that Octo-Base is more arm-texture-sensitive than RT-1-X. The ranking and physical checks support informative policy comparisons within these tested robot setups.

pairs.A: To align controller action effects, SIMPLER replays actions from existing real demonstrations in SAPIEN implementations of Google Robot and WidowX tasks. It compares real and simulated end-effector translation and rotation, then uses simulated annealing to tune controller stiffness and damping; this step requires no new demonstrations. Visual Matching tackles the visual gap by compositing segmented simulated robots and interactive objects with inpainted real backgrounds and adjusting textures. Alternatively, Variant Aggregation randomizes visual environments and averages policy outcomes across them. Existing generalist policies are evaluated in paired real and simulated settings. Mean Maximum Rank Violation penalizes pairs that simulation misorders using their real-world success-rate margins: it takes each policy's worst such margin and averages across policies. Lower values indicate better ranking agreement; Pearson correlation provides a complementary measure.
pairs.B: SIMPLER compares existing policies after reducing differences between simulated and real action effects and visual observations. For control alignment, system identification replays actions from existing real demonstrations, measures differences in end-effector translation and rotation, and uses simulated annealing to tune controller stiffness and damping. Visual Matching combines segmented simulated robots and interactive objects with an inpainted real-scene background, then adjusts or projects textures to better match real appearances. Variant Aggregation instead averages outcomes over randomized visual variants. Existing policies are evaluated on real Google Robot and WidowX setups and their SAPIEN counterparts, mainly for rigid-body tasks. Mean Maximum Rank Violation assigns each policy the largest real-world success-rate margin of a misordered policy pair involving that policy, then averages over policies. Lower values indicate closer ranking agreement; Pearson correlation separately measures linear association.

pairs.A: Visual Matching agrees more closely with real-world policy ordering than Variant Aggregation or validation action mean squared error in the Google Robot comparison. Across six checkpoints and three task groups, average Mean Maximum Rank Violation is 0.056, 0.143, and 0.375, respectively. This metric penalizes misordering by real-world success-rate margins, so the lower value favors Visual Matching as a ranking signal. Corresponding mean Pearson correlations are 0.924, 0.778, and 0.308; linear agreement and margin-aware ordering therefore favor the same approach. A complementary behavioral check asks whether simulated visual sensitivity appears on hardware: simulation indicates greater arm-texture sensitivity in Octo-Base than RT-1-X, and new real robot arm-wrapping experiments support that relative difference. These findings support relative performance evaluation and policy-specific visual sensitivity analysis in the tested robot setups.
pairs.B: Visual Matching gave closer average agreement with real-world policy rankings than Variant Aggregation or validation action mean squared error for six checkpoints across three Google Robot task groups. Mean Maximum Rank Violation penalizes incorrect ordering by real-world success-rate margins; it averaged 0.056, 0.143, and 0.375 for these approaches, respectively, with lower values indicating closer agreement. This comparison favors directly matching appearance over averaging randomized visual variants for the tested ranking task; action prediction error was a weaker ranking signal. A complementary behavioral check linked simulated sensitivity to a physical intervention: simulation suggested that Octo-Base was more sensitive to arm texture than RT-1-X, and new real arm-wrapping experiments supported that relative sensitivity. The evidence supports policy ranking and relative robustness comparisons in the evaluated setups, while some checkpoints remained sensitive to visual differences. Agreement therefore does not establish exact reproduction of physical success rates.
